That we adopt and concur in the report of the committee not by way of asking the country for a specific amount or for any amount, but as a method of forming a rough estimate of the financial handicap under which every returned man is labouring and we authorize Brother Hunter to transmit the report to Brother Colonel Currie, M.P., with a request to place the same before the Parliamentary Committee with a view to having the honourable gentlemen composing that body investigate and make their own calculations from the materials which they can obtain from evidence submitted and from data in the possession of Government departments.
We do not want you to take our calculations; we want you to make them yourselves. It is like the boy who was working on the fourth proposition of Euclid. He said he did not believe it, and the master said, "I do not want you to believe it; I want you to prove it."
By the Chairman:-Q. Boiled down, colonel, your plan suggests the payment of a cash gratuity, or the payment of money?-A. Well, I did not put it in the form of a proposition ; I was rather building a concrete base on which you could build any proposition that appealed to the committee. I know a committee starts out with the idea perhaps that they won't have to give much, or do much, but a fair-minded committee often finds itself in the position of recommending a good deal more than it was intended to recommend. Then they go back and meet people in their own part of the country who will say, "You are giving these soldiers too much." The answer is, "We are not giving them anything; we are just letting them have a little bit of their own back." That is the object.
Q. The object is rather to show a condition that must be met? A. A condition that in all fairness should be met to some extent any way, and it is not eleemosynary. You can do but something in the interests of a fair career for the man who has come back.
By* Mr. McLean :-Q. As I understand it, you have reduced in this report our indebtedness to them in dollars and cents? A. Approximately.
By the Chairman:-Q. Did you ever consider this phase of it when discussing your report that within a year after war broke out, during the whole period, right down, I think we can say, to the present time, there is scarcely a branch of labour that did not put up the plea that the wage it was receiving was a less wage, so far as the value of the dollar is concerned, than they received prior to the war?-A. Yes, I am aware of that; I am also aware that the average working man or working woman is

living on a scale of extravagance for the last three years, such as the well-to-do people would have been afraid to show ten years ago.
Q. Would it be fair to put it this way from your standpoint:	that when our organized
labour bodies throughout Canada under these conditions are agitating for higher pay and higher wages there is no foundation for their claim?

A. Only if you want every one in the country to be a sort of an aristocrat. If these people had lived on " mulligan " and things like that, which our fellows lived on, they would not have had much complaint about the wages and they would have saved lots of money. Let us take a concrete case., Take the man living on a wage of 45 cents an hour. We had examples of that; these men actually come forward, their organizations come forward, and they say that the wage of 45 cents an hour that we have been getting and are getting now is not a living wage, that the money we get now will not go as far as the same amount of money went before the war. That is the contention, and has been during the whole war period. There is considerable truth in it, and while we are at it, while the representatives of the Government are complaining that it would be difficult to get the money for such a thing as we are suggesting in the way of relief, there is a very large body of business assets that iS being neglected, and it has a great deal to do with the high cost of living. Put it in the form of a parable: " If two men take off their coats to fight and the crowd gathers around, and one of these light-fingered gentlemen goes through not only the pockets of the men who have taken off their coats, tout the pockets of the crowd as well, and you catch that light-fingered man, you do not tax the wage he has made, you confiscate it, but, of course, if he should be an incorporated company and do it on a large scale, taking advantage of the necessities of the country, he is merely a profiteer, he is not a " dip." Now you have the statistics all ready, you know this, you send this roving, wandering investigation that is going through the country, and yet you have in the statistical branch of one of your departments you have the statistics of the profiteer, you have the power between the provinces and the Dominion; if the Dominion has power to confiscate, and as they have expressed their willingness to do anything to compensate the soldier, if the Government has taken advantage of that asset then we will consider anything you say about the difficulty, but * until that is done we have every reason to differ with you on the question of having no funds. But if you had taken up this question of raising prices, and divorcing bacon from eggs, there would not be any difficulty and a man could lire on 45 cents an hour.
Q. You have raised another question, a very important question, that has been brought to our attention before. But coming back to the original question your argument is based on the difference in pay which the soldier got and the wages that we pay to the various classes of people during the period of the war?-A. Yes.
Q. Our difficulty at home during the war, has been that all the working people generally, have considerable difficulty all the time to get a wage that would be equivalent, I mean in purchasing power, to that which they had prior to the war. I think I am stating it fairly?- A. Yes, that is so but for the purposes of comparison I have taken into account the average of 75 cents a day for the food of our men, their board, for their living expenses, they didn't pay

much for rent, nor would the workmen here have paid much for rent if they had slept in the places that our men had to sleep in and they could have lived on 7(5 cents a day then as well as our men did, and perhaps better, because they would have had time to look around and select tasty things. But war-time was a time of sacrifice, there was no reason why men here should not live as hard as the men at the Front lived; they were not working the same hours every day, or working under such a strain. I do not say I do not want the working men to have a maximum degree of comfort in the future, but during wartime every man should have sacrificed something.
Q. There is only one way to wage war and that is for the State to use the services of every one whether in the front line or at home. During war every one should make equal sacrifice, as far as it is possible to arrange it, but they have not done it in the past. I think if we should get into another war like this we sjiould take some steps in that direction?-A. Yes, to ration those at home as well as the soldiers.
I have read enough to show the viewpoint of one man, a colonel who is also a barrister, and the distinction he draws between the man who fought and the man who stayed at home. The report before us does not deal with the man who made the sacrifices and is still physically fit and mentally capable, but only with the disabled and necessitous cases. That brings me to my position in this matter. Notwithstanding any appearances of threats, or whatever interpretation may be given to the remarks made in this House by anybody, I am satisfied to let this Government go to an election any time they like. My position is the one I have taken before the Great War Veterans' Association in the city of Edmonton, in my own constituency. I shall not change from that position in this House, no matter what may be the consequences. I am not seeking favour, nor have I any fear. I told the committee of the Great War Veterans' Association that came to interview me with respect to this matter that I would not stand for giving any further gratuities out of the ordinary revenue of the country. The report before the House shows conclusively that no further gratuities can be granted out of the ordinary revenues of the country, and I think the soldiers accept that as a fact. What Colonel Hunter says is that there has been profiteering, and reference has been made by the chairman of the committee to profiteering. We have had Flavelles and pork barons and a number of other gentlemen who have prospered during the war, while the soldiers were sacrificing themselves to protect these gentlemen's families and their industries. The soldiers take the ground that these men should contribute something towards their re-establish-

ment, and that is not an unreasonable view when you go into the psychology of the matter. Here is a man who has been overseas for three or four years, with no care and no responsibilities, a boy once more, capable of playing, and facing death if necessary. He comes back to Canada and finds himself suddenly face to face with responsibilities and with duties to perform both for himself and his family. He asks himself, when he sees that some of those who remained at home have made fortunes while he was sacrificing himself at the front, where is the joy I had only recently? Ils it not natural for the soldier to turn round and say: These men who have made money in my absence and who keep on enjoying themselves to-day should contribute out of their earnings to the re-establishment of the soldier, no matter how the Government may get the money?
The only reason I speak to the motion of the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Andrews) is not that I take exception to the finding of the committee that no further gratuities can be paid to the soldiers out of the ordinary revenue of the country, but because there is a method of raising the* money for these men if they are entitled to further gratuities at all. Whether or not they are entitled to them is a matter for this House to decide. If the House decides that only necessitous cases can be considered as a matter of justice and right, I am prepared to submit to the superior judgment of others and abide by the consensus of opinion of the House; but if every soldier has a right to receive some compensation for the sacrifices he made on the battlefield for you and me, this report should be referred to the committee again for further consideration as to how the money can be raised.
In 1914 we had a population of 3,700,000 males under 54 years of age, and only 595,441 were called for service. If none of the methods of raising the revenue that were suggested to the committee are acceptable to this House-and I must say that some of the suggestions were treated flippantly- there is one' method that was not considered by the committee, although I suggested it to some of the members, and that is that all men who have become 21 years of age since 1914 and who did not serve their country in the war shall bear a special tax for the 'special raising of funds to defray the cost of the gratuities which are claimed by the soldiers. We have also a foreign population of 360,000 in this country. I do not know what the exact proportion of males is. Last year I put a
question on the Order Paper asking for the information, but I received no reply from the Government, These men were prevented from fighting, and even doing national service in this country. Why should they not be called on to pay a supertax for the raising of revenue either for these gratuities or for the country at large? None of them wish to avoid their duty so far as paying is concerned. One objection that may be made to this proposal is: Some men of military age have already paid a lot of money and would you call on them to pay more? I say that every man who has paid anything has got something for it. The .man who buys $20,000,000 of Victory bonds has a paying proposition. He is not performing a patriotic aot but simply making a good investment. Another objection that may be made to this scheme is that some men imay have contributed handsomely to war funds, but I say that these men have also received handsomely of the goods and gifts that are not distributed universally to all men in Canada, and were in a position to make handsome contributions. It may also be objected that the man should not be taxed who was declared medically unfit. That question has been put to me and I say, yes, he should be taxed, because he has been receiving the benefits that accrued to those who did not have to serve although they may have had a desire to do so. It may also be objected that to avoid these taxes some of these people will go to the United States. Well, if there is any large proportion of these men who did not serve in the army who, to avoid paying the small sum they ought to pay to help the returned soldier re-establish himself, would go to the United States we will be well rid of them and Uncle Sam will not receive them with open arms if he knows the reason why they are crossing the line.
We are making far too much of the fear that this man may cross the. line or leave the country because a few dollars may be exacted from him. I am not affirming that the suggestion I make in regard to this form of taxation is one that is commendable, for I have not formulated any concrete plan. But I think that it is one that ought to be considered in all its details by a committee.
There is another method of raising revenue which, so far as I know, has not been taken into consideration, and that is a documentary tax on bills of sale, transfers, chattel mortgages, lien notes, etc. The objection may be raised to this proposal that:

I am encroaching on constitutional matters, and that as the method of taxation here suggested has reference to civil rights its adoption by Dominion authority would constitute an interference with provincial jurisdiction. I do not see that there could be any objection to the provinces coming to an agreement with the Dominion as to what ought to be done in the way of taxing documents. I suggest this matter for the consideration of the House. If hon. members are of opinion that the soldier is not entitled to any more than he is getting, then I have nothing more to say. But if the House thinks that the soldiers have suffered an injury for which they should be compensated in some degree, then I desire it to take into consideration the suggestions I submit, and to consider whether it is not possible to raise the necessary moneys for the purpose of providing the gratuity which is demanded. In his agitation to-day, the mental condition of the soldier precludes any consideration of technical rules and regulations such as govern this House, and some of the soldiers before the committee were astounded at the restrictions they encountered in the way of decorum. For instance, they could not understand that this motion, for the reason that it involves a certain money expenditure, could not originate with a private member. The soldier does not care for these fine technicalities. His mind is obsessed with one thought. He feels that as there has been money for this, that and the other undertaking there ought to be money for him.
Now, if the Government had said that the soldiers had got all they were entitled to and would get no more I might have taken issue with them on that stand. At all . events, the matter wouid have been clear cut. But that is not what the report siys It says in effect:	We have dealt with a
certain number of cases, and are prepared to accept certain suggestions and make certain recommendations, calling for an expenditure of $40,000,000 or $o0,000,000. But that is as far as we can go, because we have no money to go further. Now, the soldier says to himself that the Canadian people have paid to the railways in the form of cash bonuses, loans, mileage actually constructed, and so on a total of $274,067,049.87, of which amount the Dominion contributed $218,714,318.37, the provinces $37,437,895.16 and the municipalities $17,914,836.40. In the form of land grants the railways have received 44,096,989 acres. Of this the Dominion gave 31,864,074 and the provinces 12,232,915. In the province of Quebec the fMr. Mackie.]
railways were allowed in many cases to convert their land grants into cash at the rate of 52} cents per acre, which resulted in $4,557,728 being paid in cash for land thus converted. For all practical purposes, this amount might very well be added to the cash subsidies given by the provinces. It is not practicable to indicate the money value of the various grants, but in the case of the Canadian Pacific, the Canadian Northern and one or two other roads, the amount yielded has been very large. For the year 1918 the Canadian Pacific had land sales amounting to $15,375,996 representing an average of $16.22 per acre for lands not irrigated. The amount realized during preceding years by this company cannot be stated; but it has not been less than $100,000,000. Taken as a whole, it would be a conservative estimate to place the value of all land grants to railways at $275,000,000. Indirect aid in the form of bond guarantees has been given by the Dominion and provincial government to the amount of $358,488,395. We have proceeded far enough in experience to realize that practically all ?^ese guarantees might be properly regarded as representing cash aid. It is even more serious than this; for the guarantors are obliged to pay both principal and interest. Having regard to the fact that nearly all the guarantees are for a period of fifty years, the full sum which will in the end have to be paid out of the public treasury will not fall below $800,000,000. Adding together aJll these various forms of aid to railways we have a total in round figures of $1,359,000,000. The soldier says to himself that the Dominion has given to private corporations large sums of money to enrich their directors and shareholders, and yet when they-the soldiers-demand assistance they are told that there is no money. Yesterday the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Lafor-tune), during the space of two hours, recited the litany of the wants of his constituency, and to each count he said the reply was "No money." I, too, might have recited the wants of my constituency and could have said the reply was "No money." But for private corporations, and to help the railways, there has always been plenty of money, and we have supplied in cash aid a total of $1,359,000,000.

speechtext: And there are plenty of demands, too.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF THE SPECIAL COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Yes, but if you tax the non-combatants for a period of twenty-five years, or from 21 to 45, you will get enough money out of them to pay the soldiers, and

more than the Government gave the railways. Now, in the broad plan of nationalization, under which the Dominion Government is now proceeding, we must dearly recognize the serious fact that further very large drafts will have to be made upon the public treasury. The operating deficit of the Canadian Northern for the past year has been announced as being $5,500,000. To this must be added something like $15,000,000 on account of fixed charges, making a shortage of more than $20,000,000 for the year. This, however', is not all. Very large capital expenditures will be necessary in order to bring up this road to a proper standard of efficiency, the amount having been estimated at from $100,000,000 to $150,000,000.
The Minister of Railways has told us in the House within the last ten days how much money it is going to take to put the Canadian Northern or the Canadian National where it should be. The deficit for the past year on the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Intercolonial and the other parts of the Government system is not yet known, but it is safe to assume that it will not be less than $10,000,000. The money must be found. To a certain extent I am arguing the case of the chairman of the committee and of the committee itself, but I am also arguing the case of the soldiers. There is money for these things, but there is no money for the soldiers. In a certain sense I am refuting the report which has been made by the Opposition because these extravagances, the giving of public money for the aggrandizement of private corporations and individuals, has been the weakness of all governments, it has been carried on for a long time by the Opposition, by Liberal Governments and Conservative Governments and even by this Government. If the Grand Trunk is taken over by the Government, allowance must be made for further responsibility by the Dominion treasury. We have been told that the road is in a state of bankruptcy, and the liabilities to be assumed by the Government are "substantial in character." Without fixing the balance as between net earnings and total charges it is altogether clear that some calls will be made upon the resources of the Dominion.
The situation, taken as a whole, shows a tremendous responsibility resting on the shoulders of the Dominion. But that is not all. In considering the question of what has been done to aid general transportation interests in the Dominion account must be taken of the cost of public harbours, dredging, and the aids to navigation provided by the Department of Marine. It would seem that exact figures are not available. The account runs back beyond Confederation and is nowhere to be found in such form that a precise aggregate can be stated. From reliable sources, however, it has been ascertained that the outlay on account of harbours and dredging is not less than $110,000,000. The system of lighthouses, buoys, etc., on the coastal and inland waters of the Dominion, together with annual charges for maintenance, has at least exceeded $60,000,000. We have found the money for this.
We must next consider the canal system of the Dominion. It represents a capital cost to date of $125,000,000, to which a very large sum must be added for annual maintenance. All canals are now entirely free, and have been for fifteen years past. The cost of maintenance last year was $1,700,000.
Stepping away from the matter of transportation, it must be remembered that the Dominion Government and the various provincial governments have expended an immense sum of money for the encouragement and promotion of agriculture. The farmers who are about to take their seats in this House had better take notice of some of the things that Dominion and provincial governments have done for them. The system of experimental farms is an example of what has been done by the Dominion Government. The capital outlay on that account has reached the large total of $9,000,000. The cost of maintenance is also large. Last year it amounted to a net sum of $885,000.
The development of our mineral resources has entailed a very large public expenditure. The old Geological Survey was some years ago incorporated with the new Department of Mines, and it might be said with propriety that the entire expenditure by this "department represents a public contribution towards the mineral interests of the country. The cost of this department last year was $760,000. These are aids to private individuals and corporations. The soldier tells himself that these millions of dollars have been paid by Dominion and provincial governments to aid millionaires and magnates and yet when he comes and asks that he be given assistance for the purpose of re-establishing himself, to which assistance he feels he is entitled, he is told there is no way of raising the money.
In conclusion, if the suggestion I have made in support of the motion that this matter be referred back to the committee for consideration is feasible at all, that a

tax should be levied on all men between the ages of 21 and 45, including those who may come to this country, for the purpose of raising the necessary moneys, I would ask for the favourable consideration of the House. If, on the other hand, the House is generally of the opinion that this is a case that should not be considered, that the soldier is not entitled to any further grant, except as provided for and recommended in the report, I have nothing further to do than to submit to the general opinion of the House. I submit, however, on behalf of the delegates representing the returned soldiers that they are entitled to go home feeling, whether they are or are not granted greater concessions than are fixed in the report, that every possible consideration has been given to the question of how the money can be raised for the purpose of meeting their demand.
Mr. JOHN A. CURRIE (North Simcoe): Mr. Speaker, before I proceed to discuss the report of the committee, I wish to make a few observations relative to the position of the committee itself.

speechtext: Before the hon. gentleman begins his speech, I think there is an understanding that we are to get off at ten o'clock and I would like the hon. member to regulate his conduct accordingly. He cannot finish but. he can make a fair start.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF THE SPECIAL COMMITTEE.
speechtext: It will take me at least an hour and a half, and if it is the wish of the House I will call it off until to-morrow.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF THE SPECIAL COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I think if my hon. friend would put pep in his speech he might, get through at ten o'clock. However, he had better give us the introduction.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF THE SPECIAL COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
At a meeting last Sunday in the city of Toronto I said that the members of the special committee to which this matter of gratuities had been referred had been fairly well pledged or selected before they came together to discuss this question. The Chief Whip of the Government yesterday took occasion to take me to task after which he read a long lecture as to the military records of the members of the committee. Anybody who looks over the membership of the committee will come to the conclusion that there are certain members of the committee who have war records which I do not hesitate to acknowledge. But I am sorry that in so far as I can *see by the result of its action the commit-

tee set out with the intention of bringing in a report to a large extent similar to the one which has been brought in. I entirely disagree with the committee in many cases although I must say also that it has gone very deeply into many of these questions and problems and in endeavouring to prove that the money could not be found it has placed .a great many useful facts before the House and the country.
What is the demand of the returned soldier? Very few people seem to realize exactly what he is asking for. I wish the House to bear in mind that the Great War Veterans, the United Veterans' League, the Comrades of the Great War and all those other organizations have asked for a gratuity. They have not asked for charity. They are asking for gratuity and gratuity means a grant in money or in kind which will compensate them for lost time during the war and enable them to carry on in civilian life in the future. One would be led to believe from the speeches and actions of some of the members of the committee that such a thing as a gratuity was unknown in this country. I am going to recall to the memory of the House previous gratuities granted to soldiers. Conditions in this House are generally governed by precedent and it is no new thing ta ask for a gratuity. I can understand members who are new in the House and some who are new in the country coming to the conclusion that such a thing as a gratuity was unknown in Canada and that it is a very absurd thing for soldiers who have served in this war to ask for a gratuity.
As to the granting of gratuities, for 2,000 fears the practice has been almost invariably to make such grants to victorious

Instead of giving a gratuity the committee has shown that it must grant them charity. Assuredly, our injured soldiers and those who are incapable of helping themselves should be granted money and we should look after them. But that should be in no sense a charity. The pension that an injured man gets is to my mind not a charity. It is a grant by the nation in recognition of his services and the losses that he has sustained on behalf of the state; and to give money of that kind and consider it charity seems to me futile. It is not charity, it is a gratuity and a thing he is certainly entitled to.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF THE SPECIAL COMMITTEE.
speechtext: What is there in the report of the committee that indicates the soldier is being given anything that savours of charity?

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF THE SPECIAL COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman will read the report he will notice there is a suggestion that money should be granted to assist those that are in need during the winter, and when you speak of men as being in need you mean charity. That is all I have got to say about that feature of the report, beyond stating that that is largely the attitude of the committee in the matter.
Now, we will discuss briefly on what occasions this country has granted gratuities to soldiers. In a retrospect like this I do not need to go back to the war of 1812, although I understand grants of land were made to Canadian soldiers who served in that war. (In some of our counties are still to be found the descendants of those men who fought in the war of 1812 and who are holding lands in the province of Ontario that were given as a gratuity by the Crown for service in that war. But I will come to a later day and consider what was done in the case ol the Fenian Raid. The Fenian Raid was but a small war and not a very large number oi men were called out. I think that in the province of Ontario possibly ten or fifteen regiments were under arms altogether; I forget the exact number, but the late Minister of Militia, if he were here, could give us the exact number, 'but in any case it is immaterial so far as that goes. It was not until, I think, the session of 1912 or 1913 that this House granted a cash gratuity to all the men who had served in the Fenian raid. No question at all was raised as to how the veterans had served, or where they had served, or whether they served twenty-four hours or twenty-four months. If they served, they got that gratuity. In the province of Nova Scotia -and the leader of the Government and other hon. gentlemen who come from that province will bear me put in this statement -the Governor called out the whole population en mass, and every man so called out that was still alive when the grant was sanctioned got the gratuity without any question. Now this House made no complaint with respect to the Fenian Raid gratuity. The gratuity was freely granted and without any question, and it was a cash gratuity. We now come to the next war, and that was the Northwest Rebellion. After that war had terminated the soldiers who had served in it were given a gratuity in the shape of land-a land scrip. Now
so far as that land scrip is concerned-I think it is called "red-backed scrip"-it was worth five or six years ago three or four thousand dollars at the very least to those men. Some of this scrip in the Northwest that sold first for $100 or a pony was afterwards bought for $4,000 and $5,000; it has greatly appreciated in value until it is worth now, I understand in some cases, $6,000 or $7,000; I know of one case where $6,000 was paid for Northwest scrip. There was no grumbling whatever in the case of the Northwest grants either; the State gave the grant and was well satisfied to do so. The province of Ontario supplemented the grant to the Fenian Raid veterans by giving them one hundred and sixty acres of land up in the North country. In the case of one man who got such a grant, I understand it sold for something like $15,000 to $20,000, if not more. In this manner the State dealt with the veterans of the Fenian Raid with the veterans of the Northwest Rebellion. Now, we come to the South African War. When that war terminated and the question of recognition was raised, I was a member of this Hous'e. The South African War veterans were granted one hundred and sixty acres of Government land to be selected by them in the Northwest, plus another one hundred and sixty acres granted as an addition to their homestead, making a total grant of three hundred and twenty acres to each man. No objection was taken by this House to those gratuities. They were gratuities, and not charities at all-they were grants made to the soldiers for their services. So I say that when the soldiers who have fought in the recent great war are asking this Parliament for gratuities, they are not asking for anything new; it is no innovation but something they are justified in asking.
Now this committee has gone into the subject, and the answer it has given to the soldiers in most cases-and the only answer to the question at all-is: " We are quite willing to grant you a gratuity, but the finances of the country will not permit it." That is the point I am now coming to; I have no desire to enter upon any other point and to unduly prolong the debate on this matter. The Minister of Immigration and Colonization has discussed the whole subject very thoroughly to-day. He has shown what the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, the Soldiers' Settle- ment Board, and all these other departments that are working for the returned soldier, have done. One of the things that

we must remember is that these bureaus were all prepared and goit ready for the returned soldier; but when he came back to Canada he found the " cushy " civilian, who had remained at home, sitting in a big fat job ready to receive him, and when the soldier comes looking for something to do there is really nothing available for him as far as these positions are concerned. Take the case of the Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment in the city of Toronto; take the engineering staff of the building on College street that are dealing with the *soldiers in the province of Optario, and what do we find? There are something like six or seven men on that staff, and only one returned soldier. All of these men should be returned soldiers. I am informed that in all other parts of the country the same system obtains. The House can understand very readily that there is a good deal of grumbling on the part of the returned soldier as to what has been done as far as he is concerned. He considers he is altogether overlooked and he feels that he has a grievance against everything. He was led to believe, when he went over to the front, the promise was made to him, on the platform and elsewhere, that the State would always look after him. He comes home and instead of finding a warm welcome and a kind effort imade to assist him in every possible way, what does he find? He gets the cold shoulder and every member in this House attempting to sidestep the issue as to getting a gratuity for him.
I propose to show how that money shall be obtained. Before doing so, I want to refer to a statement made by the minister to the effect that if the House did not approve of this report the On vemmen t, would appeal to the country. It is the first time in my experience in the House of Commons-and I have been here a few years, and have been in touch more or less with the House for thirty years-that when a report is presented by the Government and they take the stand that if if was not swallowed by the House holus boius, they would resign and go to the country. I am sorry that that was done.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF THE SPECIAL COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Will the hon. gentleman permit me? I did not say any such thing. I did not say that if the report was not approved and adopted by the House the Government would resign and appeal to the country. I stated that so far as the main finding in the report was concerned- and there are a great many findings in the report-the question of the distribution of

another general grant to the soldiers, the Government could not accept the responsibility of undertaking the distribution of any such, grant.

I have no desire to make any comparisons or to name any particular members; it is not a nice thing to do. But there are members sitting on this side, Mr. Speaker, as you well know, 10 p.m. whose presence here is due entirely to the soldier vote. We are all here, virtually, as their representatives, especially we on this side; and when the soldiers ask us to assist them in reestablishing themselves, it is very poor policy for us to start out with a report such
as that which is now before us. I was very much surprised, Sir, when I read the report.
Now, I want to take up one or two of the items that the minister referred to in connection with his argument that the expenditures during the coming year were going to be so great as to make it impossible to raise the money required for a grant or gratuity. Anybody who understands the flnancies of the country knows very well that the items referred to in the report as possible difficulties in the way of making any grant are not all real difficulties. One would think that the country was bankrupt and that it was going to be impossible for us ever to raise our heads above the water. The minister points out how many millions we have to give to railways and all that sort of thing in order to carry on the business of the country for another year. For my part, I think we could omit a great many of these items for our consideration of this matter.
For instance, there is the item of public buildings, $3,000,000. I do not see any public buildings going up around the country, outside of the public buildings in the larger cities which are not included in this item. But that expenditure is on capital account and it is fair to assume that it represents an asset.
The Welland canal could very well wait for a few years. I do not see any necessity for the Welland canal enlargement for the assistance of our good friends south of the line-because they would be the chief beneficiaries of that work. Their large ships would pass through to lake Ontario and the trade that now largely goes through our canals to Montreal in the smaller-sized ships would virtually be cut out. Anyway, that is my opinion of it.

So I observe, but I hope there will not be any expenditure next year of a similar character.
Then, there is the item: "Harbour and River Improvements." Then there is the "Improvement of the St. Lawrence Ship Channel"; that is a necessity. "Shipbuilding, $40,000,000"-that is an absolute asset; the ships built in this country will be turned over to a company, and to my mind that company should be capitalized and

this amount treated as a capital expenditure. We cannot get along unless we build ships for ourselves, because every nation now is anxious to get hold of every ship it ean lay its hands on. In a fortunate- or perhaps unfortunate-moment we allowed the Imperial Munitions Board to fill our yards with ships; those ships are now over in the Old Country and are being operated by Old Country companies in the Argentine and United States trade, rather than being in this country engaged in Canadian trade. If we are to handle* our own products in their shipment to England we must have our own .ships. But that is a capital expenditure. These ships will all return tremendous profits if they are properly managed.
I am satisfied that if the Government wished to put those ships that they already own up for sale to-morrow, they would get at least 50 per cent more for them than they cost, so that they are a good investment. It is not like the railway companies, where you invest your money in them and then you have to invest more money in them to keep them going, and then pay all over * again to get them back. It is not a double investment; it is. only a single investment. The Intercolonial railway should be .included in the railway account. As regards the Quebec and Saguenay railway, that was a dead cat. subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF THE SPECIAL COMMITTEE.
speechtext: ll do not think so. I do not get stray figures very often as a rule. Apart altogether from them, as those figures have nothing to do with the question of the soldier's gratuity, if the Government wishes

to spend $100,000,000, that is no reason why the soldiers should not receive consideration, nor why they should not receive a gratuity. The Government, it is true, can go to work and spend $1,500,000,000 a year; it can buy up railways; it can buy up electric light companies; it can start public ownership schemes that will involve millions every year and then hold this up and say: Oh, we cannot do anything for the returned soldier.
I want to refer to another item in the report, and that is the soldiers' land settlement scheme. The Land Settlement Board is a most excellently managed board. The members work hard; they have a very difficult task; but the problem put forward is this: They have to settle the soldier on the land. I cannot for the world see what increased production you can get out of changing the ownership of the land. The policy adopted throughout Canada is this. A soldier selects a piece of land that is occupied already by a farmer, possibly some old farmer who wants to leave and go to live in the town and talk " U. F. O." or some other kind of politics. This Government steps in and buys that land from the farmer, and the farmer goes and lives in a village or town, so that we have lost that man's production. We have not gained any more by the deal than we had before. We simply substitute one man for another. The manner in which the Government deals with these men is not as good as the Australian scheme. When a man takes up land under our Soldiers' Settlement Act, his wife can sell the eggs, but she cannot sell the chickens without the consent of the Government, and a man who owns a farm of that kind is a thousand times worse off than an Irish tenant. The manner in which that land should be given to the soldier is this. The land should be purchased, and it should be rented on a long-term lease to the soldier with the option on his part to purchase it at the end of the term. That is the system that is suggested in Australia, and it is a system that, I think, would appeal to every hon. member in this House. If the man does not succeed on the farm, and if he leaves it, the Government has the farm and can lease it to another soldier or sell it or do whatever it likes with it. As it is now, the man goes on to the land, and-he is tied up under sixteen hundred different regulations, so that he cannot sell his crop, or a chicken, or a cow, or anything else off that farm unless he gets the consent of the Government. If that is not paternalism gone mad, I do not know anything. That is the consideration the Government gives to the returned soldier, and it is no wonder that he growls.
The question was brought up in the House by the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. Mc-Gibbon) with reference to those men who are in hospital under the demobilization scheme, who have left the military hospitals and who have gone over to the hospitals under the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment Department. Those men went under the distinct promise that the pay of their rank would be given to them. And this committee goes to work, and simply on the suggestion of somebody they want' to cut the pay of the officers down to $60 a month.
The minister would not discuss with the House the various suggestions made as to how the money Could be raised, although the House, I think, would have liked to hear from the minister the suggested form of taxation discussed. The leader of the House is, I know, very deeply interested as a student of economics, and I hope he will follow the discussion along these lines.
I will try.

The first suggestion that came before the committee was that of State lotteries, and the suggestion was made by Mr. Flynn. The suggestion is now under consideration in England with reference to a premium bond. A premium bond is, of course, a lottery, and every nation in Europe, I think, with the single exception of Great Britain, has premium bonds and has sold premium bonds and part of its debt is carried by premium bonds. That is to say, you purchase the bonds which pay interest at three and-a-half or four per cent, but a certain sum, like added interest, is set apart every year and there is a drawing, and if you have a bond and your number is fortunate enough in that drawing, you may have $500 or $1,000 or $2,000 or $10,000 in cash as a prize, but you have your bond still and you may be lucky again next year. And in the end you get your money in full back.
That is one method of getting money, and it is a cheap and easy way. While the people of Great Britain have always considered it gambling, other countries, like France, for instance, have not, and have raised large sums of money by that scheme. Then there are the Sunday theatres and liquor sales. I do not expect that we will ever get anything more from the sale of liquors. We have lost $12,000,000 or $14,000,000 through the exercise of

bone-dry laws. The inheritance tax belongs to the provinces. The ex-Minis-ter of Finance in giving evidence before the committee discussed these various questions with great clearness and force. He pointed out in the first place that the backbone of all the revenue of the country was the customs duties, but nobody asked him Whether the customs duties could not be increased. Why the absolute silence? Was it because everybody in the room was a free trader? I belong to a party that would not be afraid to add to the customs duties if it was going to produce more revenue, that was necessary. The ex-Minister of Finance went on to say that the income tax in Canada was greater than in any other country in the world practically, at least of the Allies.
No.
That may be a mistake. The income tax in this country is certainly greater than in the United States. I think that is what he intended to say.
That is what he did say.

But one would have inferred what I said just now. Not only have we as great an income tax as the United States, but we have also a tax on business profits, so our taxes on income are much greater than in the United States. I can quite understand a gentleman who is steeped to the eyebrows in free trade, like the hon. member for Vancouver, talking about nothing else but income tax. We never knew an income tax in this country until a few years ago and always raised our revenue by customs duties. We always found it a good method. The war enabled the Government to force a direct tax on the people, but I say you cannot keep that direct tax on the people more than five or six years longer, because they are going to get tired of it. Do you wonder why the farmers revolted in the last election? I can tell you. You are getting after their income. That is the chief cause of the trouble. If we continue to have an income tax in this country greater than in the United States, how in the name of conscience can we expect anybody in the United States to invest their money in Canada? Do you expect factories in this country to be enlarged or new ones to be built if you take away all extra profits? Perhaps this country can get along without additional factories. That is a question that is staring us straight in the face. We are also confronted with the question of the rate of exchange between Germany

and this country. A member of this House told me not very long ago that he wished to purchase some machines for the company he was interested in, and found that the price in the United States was something like $2,500. A gentleman attached to the company in the United States, who was a German, said, " Let us see what we can get this machinery for from Germany." They got a price around $450 or $480 on account of the drop in the value of the mark and the difference in wages. If you are going to leave our walls down to the Germans and allow the Swiss and the Dutch and the Spanish, to ship German go ids in as their own, you will deprive the factories of this country of their labour. The workingman of this country has something to say. The people who live in the cities and towns constitute 60 per cent of our population. Jf you are going to pursue a burdensome policy and grind a man down with income taxation, our manufacturers will be driven to the United States. The manufacturer who has a few hundred thousand dollars to invest and considers putting it in a factory-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I can understand that
a reference to taxation proposals is inseparable from this measure, but it does not follow that we should have a Budget debate.

tariff. But the people who are profiteering in trade in Canada are the Americans. They are the people who are sending in millions of dollars' worth of automobiles and other luxuries such as silk and diamonds. Now, most of these luxuries are free. Why should diamonds be free? Silks have a lower duty than almost anything else, and there is no reason why the luxurious articles should be almost free whilst there is a duty on woollens; it is a most absurd proposition. The customs revenue should be increased in some way, and I want to inform this House that the soldier is quite up-to-date ' and knows all about these matters. He knows very well that the country can raise additional revenue to provide the money for him. But with all your groanings about the income tax, all that can be raised in this direction is $12,000,000 or $14,000,000.
The estimate is $30,000,000.

Well, they did not raise
that last year, and it is like all the rest of the estimates in connection with the income tax in this country. They always estimate that they are going to get twice as much as they get in reality. We have not in this country men with great incomes. The country is not old enough, and while there may be a few scattered individuals with large incomes from railway stocks, it is absurd to think that you can raise revenue in this country by a taxation of incomes. The revenue to provide the gratuity must be found by means of the tariff.
Now, hon. gentlemen may think that I am talking from the standpoint of a hardshell protectionist Tory, but it was [DOT] the Conservative party that went into the war boldly because it knew that the revenues of the country could stand the strain, and that the patriotism of the people would prove equal to the task. I am very sorry that that party is not in power to-day, because I am satisfied that it would have courage enough to apply a system of protection and a national policy that could easily raise the amount that it demanded by the soldiers. If the tariff were increased I would not be afraid to take the platform in any constituency in this country, especially if there are any factories in it-
Any what?

Factories-and hold up
the banner of a national policy, and although the hon. gentleman (Mr. McMae-ter) is a free trader, I am satisfied that if the soldiers' necessity were presented clearly and fairly, he himself would be quite

willing to endorse an addition to the tariff to see these deserving men through. Why, Sir, have we no responsibility to these men? Did we promise them nothing, and are they entitled to nothing but jeers and laughter from this House? I stood in the trenohes with them and I know their feelings, and I know what were their expectations. I recruited a great number of them, and they always, in the tightest corners in France, heard a soft whisper of gratitude which they would experience on their return to the country which they were in the battle line to defend.
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question?
I wish the hon. member would not interrupt me.
I have a right to interrupt you, and I desire to ask a question.

speechtext: The hon. member has no right to ask a question without the consent of the member who has the floor.
I rise to a question of privilege.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member cannot rise to a question of privilege' while another member has the floor.
I can stand interruptions from any one who gave hostages to the country.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
The hon. gentleman is making a cowardly attack when he makes that statement in reference to myself.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. II must ask hon. members to bear in mind-
I sent my only son to the war and he stayed until the war was over.
I am quite willing to give the hon. gentleman credit for that, but the hon. gentleman belonged to a profession whose services were badly needed in the war and he could have served without trouble.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
Permit me to say that I offered my services and they were refused.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must ask hon. members to bear in mind that there is a specific resolution before the House, and it would be well to adhere to it.
You will bear me out, Mr. Speaker, that I did not occasion the interruption.
You made a cowardly attack.
You are all the time at that game.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
I can take care of you-
That is all right.
-before this debate is through.

The hon. gentleman can go ahefd and discuss anything he likes, but I have never interrupted him in my life in this House, and, indeed, I very seldom interrupt any hon. member unless I desire to get a point cleared up. That is a fact, and I wish it clearly understood. Now, Mr. Speaker, I was going to say that the ypung men who went and served in the war did so in the sanguine expectation that their country would stand behind them when the struggle was over.
They did not expect that they were going to come back here and see the very first request they placed before the House of Commons thrown down. All the time they were in France the one thing that sustained them constantly was the idea that their country was grateful for their service and that it appreciated what they were doing. There are fathers here who know, from letters from their sons, that that was the underlying principle of it all. These young men went over and offered themselves up as a sacrifice to their country. No man who has never been under fire for the benefit of his country can fully understand what that means, and God knows Canada did not go into this war to make any money out of it. We are not going to get hardly anything out of the Germans. We did not expect any territory. We went into the war purely for the sake of humanity, and these young men, for the sake of humanity, fought for the cause of liberty and freedom. We who stand here as the representatives of that liberty and freedom which has been handed down through the generations should be the last people to say that all sources of revenue are exhausted when there are many ways in which further money can be raised whereby some gratuity can be given to these soldiers. In deciding to pay a gratuity we are not instituting anything new. We are only carrying out the old established principle in this country that a man who goes to war and returns shall receive a gratuity. Never has any man gone to war from Canada who, on his return, has not received a gratuity. The gratuity has been given in Canada in lieu of what is known in England as half pay. It is only right that that should be. When these men were taken from thewar, on their way over and after they reached here, when they were receiving a gratuity, they were liable to be called upon again, every one of them. They were not released bcause they might be called upon at any time.
They had all been discharged.
They were discharged afterwards, but they were liable to be called on at any time.
That is not correct.
I know the regulations as well as the hon. gentleman does, and his statement is not correct. It was understood that they should ibe under control before they received their discharge.
Not in all cases.

The question of discharge in so far as the country is concerned has been removed from the old idea altogether. In so far as England is concerned, when a man enlists he makes a contract with the King, just the same as if he were making a contract to dig a ditch, and that contract exists until such time as he is discharged. In this country we assume that every man must go to the front if necessary. It is not a question of contract at all. Under the Military Service Act everybody becomes in reality a conscript and he is liable now, at this moment, to be called again. There is no question about that. For these reasons I think the House will be very ill advised unless it gives further consideration to this matter. I am quite willing to support the amendment of the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Andrews) if it is wide enough to include all kinds of gratuities. Do I understand it to be so from the hon. gentleman?
Men who served less than six months are not entitled to the gratuity.
At home?
At home.

That is quite correct. I
am quite willing to support that motion and I desire to say to the House that lam willing to accept any reasonable proposition that may be put before us. I am quite willing to abide by my position in this



House. I shall therefore support the amendment of the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg.
On the motion of Mr. Edwards the debate was adjourned.

In order that we may readily resume the discussion of the report which has been under consideration to-day I beg to move:
That the consideration of the fourth and final report of the special committee to which was referred Bill No. 10 an Act to amend the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment Act, and the amendment of Mr. Andrews, shall be the first order of the day at the next sitting of the House.
Motion agreed to.

At the present time there is in operation an Order in Council passed under the War Measures Act which gives to the minister the powers that arfe set forth in this resolution and upon which it is proposed to found a Bill. It is the experience of the department that in Canada at the present time there is a great shortage of certificated masters and mates. That was always the case in recent years but the condition has been much accentuated by reason of the war. During that period it transpired that very few' young men presented themselves for examination for masters' and mates' certificates. The consequence is that to-dhy in maritime ports it is frequently impossible
fMr. Currie.]
for the owners of a ship to obtain certificated officers. The proposal in this resolution gives to the minister authority for one year to enable a ship to depart without a certificated pilot if satisfied that the person proposed to be put in Charge of such a ship by the owner is competent.

I think that when the [DOT]minister looks around and sees so few members of the committee present he will agTee with me that this is not the occasion for considering so important a subject as he suggests to the committee at the present time.

My only purpose in asking the House to allow this resolution to pass is that the Bill may be printed. Every opportunity will be given for the discussion of the Bill when it is printed, but I desire' to have it on the Order Paper when we conclude the discussion on the report which is at present before the House.
_Mr. McKENZIE: I have only to say to my hon. friend that I could not at any stage agree to this resolution. It may not be so startling to a man who lives in Manitoba or Saskatchewan, or somewhere where they are not so acclimatized to this very thing as a man who lives on the coast like my6elf. It w'ould be just as reasonable for the hon. gentleman to say that if in the city of Winnipeg, for instance, there was a scarcity of doctors a particular member of the Cabinet should have authority to appoint any number of doctors to start out on surgical operations and everything that pertains to the profession of a duly-qualified medical man. The sea-captain takes charge of the ship. He has under his control a certain number of men, not necessarily passengers, that put their lives in his hands, and he sets out to sea with his thousands of dollars worth of property and precious lives. The property in his charge, and the lives of those men, depend upon his skill as a navigator and as a man who knows the theory and practice of navigation. I cannot possibly be a consenting party to putting the lives of those men and that property into the hands of a man who is not qualified under the Act. Everybody knows that the qualifications required under the Act are very simple. It is a simple thing to pass the examination and even if it is necessary to lower the standard of that examination that is another matter; but I cannot by any possibility agree to opening the door and giving such favour to .a minister who may

know nothing at all about the requirements of seamanship-
Who may be a paint manufacturer.

Possibly a paint manufacturer; at any rate he is called upon to know whether a man is a qualified seaman. A man may be aloft on a ship and a person down below who is ignorant about seamanship may swing a yard or a boom in such a way as to throw the man aloft perhaps a hundred feet away from the vessel by not knowing how to pull the right rope-in fact not understanding his business. Our whole salvation in matters of this kind is that the law requires certain experience and certain training in seamanship before a man can take charge of a vessel. Now as far as I am concerned -although the legislation may be passed over my head-I wish the minister would distinctly understand this: That I would not put the lives of the men in these ships in the hands of a man who was not a competent navigator. Speaking personally I would not go to sea with a man that I knew had not the proper training and the proper qualifications for the trust that is reposed in him.

There are two sides to the question involved in this resolution. The hon. gentleman has taken one side, but there is another aspect to be considered. It is not proposed that the minister should exercise the authority, if such power is granted him, of -putting a ship under the control of an incompetent man. The purpose of this legislation is primarily to enable sailing ships to depart from a port with out a certificated master or mate. I would like to tell my hon. friend that in the United States sailing ships up to 700 tons can sail anywhere the world over without certificated masters, or mates. In Great Britain where they have had a century of experience in such matters, they do not require masters and mates to be certificated in sailing ships in the coasting trade-
In all sailing ships?

-and I do not think they require certificated masters and mates in ships of a certain size sailing coastwise in Great Britain. I was discussing this matter only yesterday with the officers of the Department of Marine and we were seriously contemplating bringing forward at this stage a Bill to enable Canadian sailing ships to sail anywhere without certificated masters and mates. No owner will
113i
allow his ship to depart from port in the hands of an inexperienced man. This, of course, does not relate to passenger boats. I think myself we might very well abandon the idea of requiring certificated masters and mates for sailing ships, particularly up to a certain tonnage. I really think we will have to do that, otherwise the sailing marine in this country will not be able to get the men. They have not been able to do so during the war fand frequently the department, in order that a ship could depart from a port, has been obliged to exercise the power given the minister under the War Measures Act, but which we wish to perpetuate for another year. Only to-day I was in receipt of a telegram from Halifax with respect to two sailing ships that were ready to depart but were unable to obtain certificated officers. They could not get them and they were advised that if the Customs officer at the port would certify that they had made diligent efforts to secure certificated officers, they would be permitted to depart upon furnishing an experienced man. I appreciate that there is something in the argument of my hon. friend. The only thing I ask of him is to permit the resolution to pass in order that the Bill may be printed, subject to the understanding that it will not in the slightest degree prejudice him in the matter of the right of discussion.

I would suggest to my hon. friend that if he is doing this with a view of hastening the passage of this legislation through the House, he is not wise. I realize the full force of what he has said as to the difficulty of obtaining certificated officers, and I can quite understand there may be circumstances in which it may be necessary to sanction these exceptional cases in order to carry on the trade and commerce of the country. But I think we ought to let the public know that this Bill is proposed, and possibly we would discover that there is not as much difficulty in some quarters in getting competent men as is alleged. It may be that there are many shipmasters who are willing to give their services, but possibly the conditions offered to them are not satisfactory. I am rather in sympathy with the objects of the Bill but I would strongly advise my hon. friend not to rush it through but to allow full opportunity for the discussion of the measure.

I do not propose to rush the Bill through, I simply wanted to advance it a stage so that it can be

printed. We cannot reach it, in any event, for two days.

But two days is a very limited time to allow for a measure which affects so many people. I think the maritime population of our country ought to be made aware that there is such a Bill and if there are any certificated officers around who are unemployed, but who, for some reason or other, do-not seem to suit the owners, they should have an opportunity of making their position known. It is true that of late years there have been very few young men coming up for examination. Nevertheless there are a good many veteran shipmasters still around our coasts and before agreeing to the Bill-I do not object to the hon. gentleman's motion-I should like to be satisfied that all these people will have the opportunity of getting employment, and it is only in case such qualified men are not available that the provisions of the Bill will be carried out.

speechtext:
Shall the resolution
carry?

I am sure the minister knows as well as I do that one of the proudest and most honoured professions in our province is that of shipmaster, and those who have reached a high position in that calling and take pride in their profession, are men to whom we look up. I cannot understand therefore why we are now proposing to cut that education down and say to the shipmaster, or to the man who wants to qualify himself, " Oh, your position is a picayune one. Anybody can sail a ship; what are you talking about? I am going to put this boy in charge of a vessel; he can take her to Newfoundland and across to Liverpool; it is all camouflage'to say that it is necessary to have a qualified man on this job." That may be said, but it is not the fact. It requires education, practice and skill to fulfil such duties, and to pass this Bill is to belittle the importance that we have hitherto attached to the profession of seamanship. I should be very much surprised to learn that the law in England is as my hon. friend says it is. The last Shipping Act passed in England, the Act of 1894, is also in force here. Our own Shipping Act is more or less supplementary to it, and when our Act conflicts with the English Act of 1894, in many cases the English Act prevails. I shall be surprised if my hon. friend can show me a provision in the Shipping Act of 1894 to the effect that shipmasters require no certificates. It has been the

boast of our men in Nova Scotia that they had to pass the British Board. A man might get a Canadian certificate, but he was not half as proud of that as he would be of a certificate received from the British Board of Trade, which is the creme de la creme of qualification as a seaman. Ilf that is all gone, I have not been aware of it.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
